entry.title: R3 Robotics
entry.summary: R3 Robotics builds robots that take EV batteries apart to recover the materials and components inside. We repositioned the company around recovering value and created an identity that behaves the same way: a custom wordmark with removed segments, modular graphics that separate and reassemble, and 3D exploded views that reveal what’s hidden inside.
entry.content:
Autor(es): Artur Zawiasinski, Grzegorz Leśniewicz, Leszek Jańczyk, widehue.co ⁣

R3 Robotics builds robots that take EV batteries apart to recover the materials and components inside. We repositioned the company around recovering value and created an identity that behaves the same way: a custom wordmark with removed segments, modular graphics that separate and reassemble, and 3D exploded views that reveal what’s hidden inside.




Making circularity work
R3 Robotics partnered with us to redefine its brand as it evolved beyond battery disassembly into a broader robotics platform for intelligent value recovery. Our goal was to create a future-proof identity that positioned the company as a trusted industrial technology partner.



Scope of work 
→ Naming: Anna Romańska
→ Brand strategy: Artur Zawiasiński
→ Brand design: Artur Zawiasiński
​​​​​​​ → 3D Visuals: Clement Begue, Maciej Kamycki, Michał Topolewski
 → Motion design: Michał Topolewski, Maciej Kamycki, Leszek Jańczyk
 → Web design: Grzegorz Leśniewicz
→ Webflow: Sławomir Buczyniak



Brand strategy
Circular economy relies on recovering value before products become waste. Through intelligent robotic disassembly, R3 Robotics enables valuable components and materials to remain in circulation.

Rather than positioning R3 around recycling though, we built the brand around dissasembly as Recovering Value. It speaks the language of manufacturers, OEMs, and industrial operators by focusing on efficiency, return, and economic value rather than waste.

entry.title: SKELTCH Business Stationery
entry.summary:
SKELTCH explores the moment when ideas first appear on paper.
The identity is built around a dynamic wordmark that behaves like a piece of typed text, constantly shifting, rearranging and forming new compositions. Its unconventional structure reflects the spontaneous nature of creative thinking, where ideas emerge, overlap and take unexpected directions.
This approach became the foundation for the packaging design. A vivid orange palette creates an expressive and instantly recognizable visual presence. The wordmark is enhanced with a dimensional 3D finish, turning typography into a tactile element that extends beyond the printed surface.
The result is a visual identity that feels energetic, unconventional and unapologetically bold. SKELTCH transforms everyday stationery into an expression of creativity, where even the simplest blank page holds the potential for something new.

entry.title: PARASOMA
entry.summary:
PARASOMA is a research project we’re developing at NastPlas on the body an organism would have if it were formed by two biological systems in a stable association. What interests us is the boundary between them: one region densifies because it has to bear tension, another stretches into a membrane, an interface thickens until it becomes a compartment.
We start from documented phenomena (lichenization, extracellular matrix, endosymbiosis, differential growth, structural color) and turn them into organizational rules. What comes out of those rules is speculation, and we keep it carefully separate from what has been established. None of these forms exist, but each one should be explainable.
There are 21 open series. Each starts from a hypothesis, carries its own risk and its own palette, and we discard a lot.
As the research moved forward, the rules started to feel too limited for a still image. So we developed two applications that are part of the project.

entry.title: Written Faces: portraits made of words
entry.summary: A picture is worth a thousand words? Seven portraits made of the writing that belonged to each life: Cavafy's manuscripts, Bach's scores, Beethoven's conversation books, petitions signed against slavery and for women's vote, Kallirroi Parren's newspaper and Florence Nightingale's letters. Stills, close-ups and films by Charis Tsevis.
entry.content:
Autor(es): Charis Tsevis

A picture is worth a thousand words? Seven portraits made of the writing that belonged to each life: Cavafy's manuscripts, Bach's scores, Beethoven's conversation books, petitions signed against slavery and for women's vote, Kallirroi Parren's newspaper and Florence Nightingale's letters. Stills, close-ups and films by Charis Tsevis.

Written Faces
A picture is worth a thousand words?
Portraits made of the words that made them.

Handwriting is the most personal trace a person leaves. It keeps the pressure of a hand, the speed of a thought, the pause before a word. Before anyone reads it, it is already a portrait.

Each face here is made of writing that belonged to that life. Some of it is testimony of the soul: Cavafy’s manuscripts, Bach’s scores, the notebooks in which Beethoven’s friends spoke to him once he could no longer hear. Some is testimony of courage: thousands of names under petitions against slavery in Massachusetts and for women’s vote in New Zealand, signed when putting your name to a cause was a public act. And some is testimony of ideas, like the newspaper Kallirroi Parren founded to argue for the education and work of women.

From across the room each portrait is a likeness. From twenty centimetres it comes apart into notes, words and names that can still be read. Sometimes a person is drawn in their own hand; sometimes the many who wrote together form the face of the one who moved them.

That is the idea behind the series: our words make who we are and trace the road we take. It is still being written, and these seven faces are only its first pages.
C. P. Cavafy
1863–1933 · The soul · his manuscripts

The Alexandrian poet wrote, revised and copied his poems by hand, and for most of his life shared them only on loose sheets and in small private collections. His face is made of his own handwriting, cut from manuscript pages in dark ink: drafts and fair copies of poems such as Waiting for the Barbarians and Days of 1900.

The film builds him to Elli Lambeti’s reading of «Έτσι πολύ ατένισα» (1917), a poem about looking at beauty for so long that it fills the sight.
Manuscripts: Cavafy Archive, Onassis Foundation (CC BY-SA 4.0). Voice in the film: Elli Lambeti, from the LP «Η Έλλη Λαμπέτη διαβάζει Καβάφη» (Dionysos, 1983). This portrait, its close-ups and the film’s images are licensed CC BY-SA 4.0, as the manuscripts’ licence requires.
Frederick Douglass
1818–1895 · Courage · signatures against slavery

Frederick Douglass escaped slavery in 1838 and became the most powerful voice for its abolition. In the same years thousands of people in Massachusetts, many of them women who could not vote, signed petitions to end it.

His face, after a daguerreotype of about 1855, is made of 2,903 of their signatures, cut from 194 pages of four petitions dated 1839 to 1849. Every mark in it is a name.
Signatures: Massachusetts anti-slavery petitions, 1839–1849, Massachusetts Archives, digitised by Harvard (Harvard Dataverse, antislaverypetitionsma; public domain). Portrait: daguerreotype, about 1855, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 2001.756 (public domain). Music in the film: «Freedom» by Charis Tsevis.
Ludwig van Beethoven
1770–1827 · Ideas · his conversation books

From 1818 Beethoven could no longer follow speech, so the people around him wrote their side of every conversation in small notebooks, and he answered aloud. Friends, his nephew, publishers and strangers filled them with news, music, politics and gossip until his death.

This portrait, after Joseph Karl Stieler’s painting of 1820, is made of 764 words in pencil and ink, taken from the first page of each of the 136 notebooks digitised in Berlin.
Words: Ludwig van Beethoven, Konversationshefte, Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin, Mus.ms.autogr. Beethoven, L. v. 51 (Public Domain Mark 1.0). Portrait: Joseph Karl Stieler, Beethoven mit dem Manuskript der Missa solemnis, 1820 (public domain). Music in the film: Piano Sonata No. 31, Op. 110, I. Moderato cantabile molto espressivo, recorded by Musopen (public domain).
Kate Sheppard
1847–1934 · Courage · the 1893 suffrage petition

Kate Sheppard led the campaign that made New Zealand, in 1893, the first self-governing country where women won the vote in national elections. Its last petition was a roll of sheets glued end to end and unrolled across the floor of Parliament.

Her portrait is made of 10,716 signatures cut from 427 sheets of that petition, each in its own ink: iron-gall brown, violet, blue-black.
Signatures: Women’s Suffrage Petition 1893, Archives New Zealand, LE1 1893/7a (CC BY 2.0). Portrait: “Mrs. K. W. Sheppard”, photograph published 1905 (public domain). Music in the film: «Heave Her Home» by Charis Tsevis.
Johann Sebastian Bach
1685–1750 · The soul · his autograph scores

Bach after Elias Gottlob Haussmann’s portrait of 1748, holding a page of music. The face is made of 4,383 fragments of his own manuscripts in six inks: staves, note heads, clefs and beams, each toned to the colour of the painting beneath it.

Up close you read the composer’s hand, never enlarged beyond the resolution of the scan.
Manuscripts: autograph scores of J. S. Bach on Wikimedia Commons (71 files, public domain). Portrait: Elias Gottlob Haussmann, 1748, via Google Arts & Culture (public domain). Music in the film: Aria of the Goldberg Variations, played by Kimiko Ishizaka (Open Goldberg Variations, CC0).
Kallirroi Parren
1861–1940 · Ideals · the newspaper she founded

Kallirroi Parren founded Εφημερίς των Κυριών in 1887, a weekly written by women for women, and edited it for three decades. It argued for girls’ education and for women’s work and vote.

Her face, after an engraving of 1889, is made of 3,562 printed words from ten issues of the paper, 1895 to 1907. The masthead words recur all over it.
Words: Εφημερίς των Κυριών, 1895–1907, digitised by Lekythos, University of Cyprus (public domain). Portrait: engraving in Ημερολόγιον Σκόκου, 1889 (public domain). Song in the film: «Προς τη Μελλούμενη Γη», music by Charis Tsevis, words by Kostis Palamas.
Florence Nightingale
1820–1910 · Care · her letters

The series could not end without the nurse who became the symbol of her profession. Of all the people who work for others, nurses are the ones Charis Tsevis admires most.

Florence Nightingale nursed the wounded of the Crimean War, walking the wards at night with a lamp, and went on to found modern nursing: the training school at St Thomas’ Hospital in London, and the statistics that showed how many soldiers died of disease rather than of their wounds.

Her portrait, after a photograph of about 1860, is made of words cut from seventeen pages of her own letters: a letter of 1883 to the probationer nurses at St Thomas’, two pages to Lt. Col. Lefroy of 1855 and a letter of 5 July 1856. Light words radiate from the lamp; black ones fall away from it like rays.

The film is a play with the light: the lamp lights, its rays reach out, and the light falls on her band by band.
Words: letters of Florence Nightingale, Wellcome Collection (Public Domain Mark 1.0). Portrait: photograph of Florence Nightingale, about 1860, Wikimedia Commons (public domain).
How they are made
Sources. Each portrait starts from a digitised archive: scans held by libraries, archives and museums, chosen page by page for dark, legible ink.

Cutting (Diakrisis). The studio’s own tools separate ink from paper. They estimate the paper beneath the writing, drop rulings and stains, and split every sheet into its units of ink: a word, a signature, a phrase of music. Each leaves as a transparent image that holds nothing but its ink.

Placing (Mozaix). Mozaix, the studio’s mosaic engine, puts every piece where its tone and shape match the portrait beneath, laying several inks one over another, the way a printer lays plates.

Finishing (Photoshop). The result opens as a layered Photoshop file, up to 12,302 × 15,000 pixels for Bach, large enough to print big and still read every word.

Films (After Effects). Because the place of every piece is known, the portrait can be rebuilt in motion. The placements go into After Effects and the studio’s render scripts, where a camera follows the pieces arriving until the face is whole.
What the cutting keeps: real pieces, one row per portrait.
A long tradition

Writing has been turned into image for as long as there has been writing. Around 300 BC Simias of Rhodes shaped his poems as an egg, a pair of wings and an axe. In the ninth century Hrabanus Maurus wrote figures into the grid of his verses in praise of the Cross. Hebrew scribes drew micrography, lines of tiny script that form borders, beasts and, by the nineteenth century, whole portraits. Islamic calligraphers turned sacred phrases into lions, birds and ships, and Chinese calligraphy has long held that the writing shows the writer. In 1918 Apollinaire’s Calligrammes let the lines of a poem fall as rain.

In 1967 Ken Knowlton and Leon Harmon at Bell Labs built a computer picture out of printed symbols, the beginning of the tradition this studio works in. These portraits belong to that line, with one difference: none of the writing was made for the picture. Every word and every name was there first, on a real page, written for its own reason.
We are open to ideas for the faces to come: tsevis.com/contact.
Artworks © Charis Tsevis, licensed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, except the portrait of Cavafy (CC BY-SA 4.0, as its manuscripts require). The source documents keep their own terms, named under each portrait.

We worked on a full brand identity renewal for BHU, creating a more distinctive, contemporary, and scalable visual language while preserving the brand’s familiar warmth and heritage. The new identity brings together tradition and modernity through a bold yet approachable system designed to work across packaging, retail environments, digital communication, and everyday customer touchpoints.
entry.content:
Autor(es): Velvele Studio

Bolulu Hasan Usta is one of Turkey’s most recognized dessert brands, known for its long-standing presence in traditional sweets, ice cream, and pastry culture. We worked on a full brand identity renewal for BHU, creating a more distinctive, contemporary, and scalable visual language while preserving the brand’s familiar warmth and heritage. The project included brand strategy, logo refinement, monogram design, typography, color system, packaging design, menu visuals, store applications, signage direction, social media assets, and art direction. The new identity brings together tradition and modernity through a bold yet approachable system designed to work across packaging, retail environments, digital communication, and everyday customer touchpoints.



Bolulu Hasan Usta

The rebranding of Bolulu Hasan Usta reinterprets a widely recognised traditional dessert brand with a strong, memory-driven identity into a contemporary design language. Present across Turkey, from east to west, and experienced by generations across diverse demographics, the brand holds a shared place in collective memory. The challenge was not visibility, but sustaining emotional continuity while restoring relevance for a new generation.

This approach extends across every layer of the rebranding, from storytelling to visual expression. With more than 40 products across multiple categories, packaging became a defining tool in structuring the brand. It evolved beyond a surface into a framework that organises complexity, introduces clarity, and maintains consistency while allowing each range to express its own character. Product categories were shaped by their nature and display context, creating an adaptable visual language.

INDUSTRY                      SERVICE              YEAR
Hospitality                        Rebranding            2026
Food & Beverage            Packaging




As the most tangible touchpoint, packaging carries both function and meaning. Traditional desserts are presented in brown tones to stand out within refrigerated environments. 
For grab-and-go items such as grissini and biscotti, transparent packaging foregrounds the product, encouraging quick and intuitive choices, while cylindrical forms enhance ease of handling.





Material and structural decisions play a central role. Pastry packaging adopts a zero-glue construction that unfolds effortlessly, supporting both ease of use and responsible production. In the chocolate range, the box opens into a floral structure inspired by “İzmir’s flowers”, a motif rooted in the city where the brand was first established. 
Widely recognised through a national song, these flowers symbolise freedom and independence associated with İzmir’s identity. By translating this cultural reference into form, the packaging turns a simple act of opening into a layered experience, connecting product, place, and memory.
